about: Who the state and federal officials outside the town are, and what weighs on their votes. Read by src/core2/officials-roster.ts and src/core2/modules/officials.ts. Every number is tagged SOURCED, ESTIMATED (with its source and spread) or TUNABLE (with the spread it's checked against). Officials are fictional people seated in the party that really holds each seat.

ideology.about: Each member's own left-right position (their ideal point) on the DW-NOMINATE first dimension, which runs from -1 (left) to +1 (right): the party's mean and spread in the 119th Congress. A member's draw follows their district: within a party, members from districts that lean further their party's way sit further out (Voteview: within-party correlation of first-dimension scores with district presidential vote about 0.4 to 0.6).
ideology.source: Voteview, HS119_members.csv (Lewis, Poole, Rosenthal, Boche, Rudkin and Sonnet, Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database, 2026), retrieved 2026-10-12: House Democrats mean -0.386 sd 0.114 (n 222), House Republicans 0.524 sd 0.160 (n 227), Senate Democrats -0.367 sd 0.106 (n 45), Senate Republicans 0.555 sd 0.168 (n 57); independents -0.546, -0.170 (Senate) and 0.152 (House).
ideology.otherSource: Independents and third parties: the mean of the three independents in the 119th Congress (-0.546, -0.170, 0.152), spread across that range; their side is then set by where their state or district leans (the same district pull as party members).

districtPull.source: Within-party correlation between a member's first-dimension score and their district's presidential vote (Voteview 117th to 119th Congresses; Bafumi and Herron 2010, APSR 104(3): about 0.4 to 0.6).

stateMeanScale.source: State legislative parties sit somewhat closer together than Congress's on average (Shor and McCarty 2011, 'The Ideological Mapping of American Legislatures', APSR 105(3): the median state's party gap is below Congress's, with wide variation by state).

executiveSpreadScale.source: Governors and statewide executives spread like the Senate's members around their party's mean (no roll calls to place them; checked against Shor and McCarty-style governor estimates that track their state's Senate delegation).

leanScale.source: Members sit further out than the voters they represent: placed on a common scale with the electorate, each party's median member of Congress is to the outside of roughly 80 to 90 percent of the national electorate (Bafumi and Herron 2010, 'Leapfrog Representation and Extremism', APSR 104(3)). The game's voter lean is a person's rank in the electorate from -1 to 1, so a first-dimension score of about -0.4 (the median House Democrat) reads as a lean near -0.8. Each party's median member then sits near the 15th or 85th percentile of voters (a lean near -0.65 or +0.85), and a member's lean is capped at the electorate's own ends (-1 and 1).

wings.about: A party's members split into three wings by where they sit within the party, in party standard deviations from its mean: the tercile cut points of a normal spread (about -0.43 and +0.43). The wing toward the other party is its moderate wing; the far wing is the liberal (Democrats) or conservative (Republicans) wing. Checked against caucus sizes: the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the Freedom Caucus each hold about a third or less of their party; the Blue Dog and Problem Solvers caucuses hold the members closest to the center.

signatureIssues.about: Each member holds a few questions as their own causes, where their view departs from their overall position (a farm-state member on trade, a member with a sick parent on health care). Which questions and how far is who the person is, drawn once from the world's seed.

count.source: Members specialize in a few issues (Hall 1996, Participation in Congress: members are active on a handful of issues outside their committees).

tiltSd.source: How far a member's view on one of their own issues departs from their overall position. Checked against the second dimension's spread within parties (Voteview 119th: second-dimension sd about 0.3 to 0.4).

independents.about: Whom each independent member of Congress caucuses with, from the public roster's caucus field. A state legislator who is independent caucuses with the party closest to their own views, unless they sit between the parties, in which case they caucus with no one.
independents.source: https://unitedstates.github.io/congress-legislators/legislators-current.json (public domain, CC0), retrieved 2026-10-12: both independent senators caucus with the Democrats; the independent House member left the Republican party on 2026-03-09 and caucuses with the Republicans.

betweenBand.source: Share of the distance between the two parties' means, either side of the midpoint, within which an independent sits between the parties and caucuses with no one. Checked against the independents in state legislatures who organize with neither party (NCSL, 'State Partisan Composition', 2026: most independents caucus with a party).

traits.about: The personality facets drawn for each official, in the same units as residents' traits, from the world's seed. Officials are drawn from people suited to public life: more outgoing, dutiful and driven than average (Dietrich, Lasley, Mondak, Remmel and Turner 2012, 'Personality and Legislative Politics: The Big Five Trait Dimensions Among U.S. State Legislators', Political Psychology 33(2): legislators score above the public on extraversion and conscientiousness).

weights.about: How much each influence weighs in a member's position on a bill. Each is a recorded reason on the member's vote. The weights together are checked against roll-call party unity: in recent Congresses about two thirds of House roll calls split the parties and the average member votes with their party on about 90% of those (CQ Vote Studies 2023 and 2024; Voteview party-unity scores).

views.source: The member's own view on the bill's questions, the yardstick the others are measured against.

district.source: How much their district's (or state's) lean on the questions weighs beside their own views. Checked against dyadic representation studies (Miller and Stokes 1963; Bafumi and Herron 2010).

party.source: Party and leadership pressure: what the party's floor leader wants, times how much the party as a whole cares about the bill. Checked against party-unity voting (CQ Vote Studies: average member unity about 90% in the House and Senate, 2019 to 2024).

caucus.source: The pull on an independent from the party they caucus with, a little less than on a party member. Checked against the two independent senators' unity with Senate Democrats (about 90%, Voteview 118th to 119th).

wing.source: The pull of the member's own wing (the Progressive Caucus, Blue Dogs, Problem Solvers, Freedom Caucus act as blocs). Checked against bloc defections on party votes (Clarke 2020, 'The House Freedom Caucus', Legislative Studies Quarterly 45(3)).

ambition.source: How much more an ambitious member answers to their district as their next election nears, and to the wider state a higher office would need. Checked against Rohde 1979 (progressive ambition and moderation) and Kousser, Lewis and Masket 2007 (members moderate before an election).

press.source: Press attention: how far a member in the public eye leans toward the side of a bill the public favors (the policy's polled national support). Checked against Arnold 1990, The Logic of Congressional Action (traceable, visible votes follow public opinion more).

independentReason.source: How much more a truly independent member weighs a bill that touches the reason they're independent (Sinclair 2006: independents and centrists build their record on a few defining issues).

loyalty.about: How strongly a member feels the party's pressure, 1 for a typical member, moved by their traits and their place in the party: dutiful and agreeable members follow the leadership more, combative and risk-taking ones less, and the leadership themselves the most (Dietrich et al. 2012; Kanthak 2007, party leadership PAC giving and loyalty).

ambitionTraits.about: How ambitious a member is, from their traits: enterprising and risk-taking people seek higher office (Fox and Lawless 2005, 'To Run or Not to Run for Office', AJPS 49(3); Maestas, Fulton, Maisel and Stone 2006).

visibility.about: How much press attention an office draws, 1 for the most watched. Checked against news coverage by office (Arnold 2004, Congress, the Press, and Political Accountability: senators get several times a House member's coverage; state legislators get little).

leadership.about: The leaders each chamber's members elect: the presiding officer and the floor leader from the majority, and the minority's floor leader. They are the party's most senior members by service (Jenkins and Stewart 2013: seniority remains the main path to leadership). Leaders are people in every state's legislature, the town's or not.

stateSample.about: For legislatures outside the town's state, the rank-and-file members are a representative sample: this many members per chamber, split among the parties by their real seat counts, each standing for an equal share of their party's members. Kept small because those legislatures act only at the coarse level today.

colleagues.about: Officials who serve together know each other: a state's delegation to Congress, and each chamber's members with their party's leader. The time they've spent together is their shared years of service at a few hours a year (delegation lunches and caucus meetings); closeness then follows the core's own closeness model.

hoursPerSharedYear.source: Delegation and caucus meetings: state delegations meet a few times a year and party caucuses weekly while in session (Congressional Research Service, 'House Leadership Structure', 2023).

maxYears.source: Shared service counted up to this many years (closeness fades between contacts in the core's model).

tierSource: Officials outside the town act on the calendar (sessions, votes, elections), not on a daily or monthly routine of their own until the player meets them.
